prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its development into incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: I have changed my third name, and I want to say why in scientific terms rather than because four colleagues prefer Knudsen. B046 remains the clear first choice: a discernible change in a field, with the mechanism confirmed independently for decades and randomized outcome evidence in glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal disease. Holst established incretin physiology and the secretion and active forms of GLP-1 in humans. Drucker defined receptor and tissue biology and carried it toward therapy. Knudsen's work turned a peptide with a minutes-long half-life into liraglutide and semaglutide, and that step is what made the discovery a medicine. The round-1 exchange moved me because the disagreement turned out to be about what the prize recognises, and the chair's summary confirms the science is not in dispute. If the citation names the physiology and its development into therapy, a trio of Drucker, Holst and Knudsen covers the full arc that this prize part is meant to recognise, and each name rests on a contribution the supplied record documents. Mojsov's contribution is real, but it is the one name whose inclusion depends on a priority claim that nobody, myself included, has verified.
statement.case_against: My earlier trio was a defensible reading of a discovery prize, and I have not shown it to be wrong. The Knudsen trio has a real weakness: Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1 peptide, and the Habener group's proglucagon work, are left outside it, and a committee that credits an industrial developer while omitting an academic discoverer can be criticised for rewarding development over discovery. The citation can state that it recognises physiology and its development into therapy, but it cannot make the exclusion of Mojsov and Habener principled on its own. A further concern is that a very expected prize of this kind could be read as a clinical-impact award. Long-term safety and durability of chronic incretin therapy for obesity are still accumulating, though that does not undermine the maturity of the core finding.

responses.point: Argued that the clinical transformation rests on the long-acting analogues, that a discovery prize stopping at the peptide omits the step that produced the benefit, and that Mojsov should replace Knudsen only if the record clearly favours her.
responses.response: I now agree with you on the substance. In round 1 I said I would move toward your trio if Mojsov's work could not be separated from the Habener group or verified, and nothing in the supplied material verifies it, so my condition is met. I also concede your point that a prize stopping at the peptide leaves out the step that produced the benefit. I do not agree that the exclusion of Mojsov is therefore comfortable. Your own recollection is, like mine, unverified, so I would not describe this as settled. I would ask that the committee record that the Mojsov and Habener question was examined and could not be resolved from the supplied record.

responses.point: Held to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov as a discovery-centred trio, and warned that agreement between two members relying on recollection is not verification, asking that the priority question be flagged explicitly.
responses.response: You were right that our agreement in round 1 was not verification, and the chair's summary confirms that the priority question is unresolved. That is the main reason I moved. A prize cannot rest its third name on a priority claim that two of us remember and nobody has checked, while the Knudsen contribution is documented. I also think your point that Knudsen's absence leaves a prize that seems to stop short of the clinical achievement it cites is correct, and it is the argument that weighed most with me. You are the most settled on Mojsov, so I would put to you directly whether you would accept the Knudsen trio if the citation names the physiology explicitly. If you hold to Mojsov, I would not call that unreasonable, and the committee should discuss it as an attribution question and not as a count.

responses.point: Proposed Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, treating Mojsov as a credit question not resolvable from the supplied text, but said he would accept a Mojsov-for-Knudsen swap if B046 is framed as a discovery prize.
responses.response: In round 1 I argued that removing Mojsov for credit difficulty while keeping a developer reverses the usual priority. I still think that argument has force, and I do not retract it. But you pointed to the right test, which is how the prize is framed, and on that test I think a physiology-and-development citation is the better reading of this achievement, because the supplied credited names and the evidence of benefit both span the full arc. Your willingness to swap if the framing changes shows we differ on citation emphasis and not on the science. I would resist only the claim that this makes the prize obviously a clinical-impact award, since Holst and Drucker are two of its three names for pure physiology.

responses.point: Said that the Mojsov-for-Knudsen swap gives a cleaner basic-science citation but leaves the clinical half resting on Drucker alone, and preferred to keep a development contributor.
responses.response: Your objection that the swap leaves the clinical half resting on Drucker alone is the one I could not answer in round 1, and I have now accepted it. I would add a caution that cuts against both our configurations: your phrasing treats Knudsen as the development half, but Drucker's work also bridged to therapy, so the arc is not cleanly divided between academic discoverers and an industrial developer. I would therefore keep the citation wording that covers the physiology and the development together, and avoid language that implies the therapies were a by-product of the physiology or that the discovery half is complete without Mojsov and Habener.

responses.point: Ranked optogenetics second as a transformative method but said six credited names cannot be resolved into a defensible trio, and rated imatinib below the unfolded protein response and CAR-T.
responses.response: I agree that no trio from B030 is defensible, and nothing in round 1 has changed that for me. On the fallbacks, I would keep B037 and B014 as alternatives in that order only for the reason that B037 has the larger demonstrated patient benefit. Both require an attribution caveat, namely Eshhar's chimeric receptor concept for B037 and the PERK and ATF6 arms for B014, and neither is a reason to add a second part to B046. I see no clear gain from a two-part configuration, and with the cap of three people in total it would force a drop of one of the B046 names.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1 peptide is independent and decisive relative to the Habener group; the supplied record does not settle it and my recollection is not verification.
Whether the committee wants the citation to state physiology and development together, which supports the Knudsen trio, or physiology only, which would favour Mojsov.
Whether B037, with Eshhar's chimeric receptor concept outside the credited names, or B014, with limited clinical translation so far, is the better fallback if the B046 allocation stalls.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict requires recusal on B046, B037 or B014. My documented collaboration with Ronald Evans (nuclear receptors) and Johan Ericson (dopamine neurons), and my co-authorship with Per Svenningsson and Abdel El Manira on other topics, do not concern any proposed laureate. As Secretary I have no documented tie to Drucker, Holst, Knudsen or Mojsov.
